scenes.heading: Food webs and energy flow
scenes.sub: Why are there far more plants than eagles?
scenes.say: Every living thing needs energy, and in an ecosystem it almost always starts as sunlight. It's passed on when something gets eaten. So why are there far more plants than eagles?

scenes.heading: Who's who
scenes.say: Producers, like eucalyptus trees, make their own food by photosynthesis. Consumers eat other organisms: a koala is a herbivore, a dingo is a carnivore, and an emu is an omnivore. Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

scenes.heading: Food chains and webs
points: Arrows show the direction of energy flow
Read the arrow as 'is eaten by'
A food web is many linked food chains
scenes.say: In a food chain, arrows point from the eaten to the eater, showing the direction energy flows. Read the arrow as 'is eaten by'. A food web links many chains together. It's more realistic, because most animals eat more than one thing.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Spend most of $100, pass about $10 on, who passes on about $1
scenes.science: About 10% of energy passes to each next trophic level
scenes.breaks: spent money still exists and can come back, but energy lost as heat leaves the food chain for good. And 10% is only a rule of thumb.
scenes.say: Imagine getting a hundred dollars of pocket money. You spend most of it and pass about ten dollars to your sibling, who passes on about one dollar. Energy works the same way. Roughly ten percent reaches the next trophic level.
scenes.caption: Imagine getting $100 of pocket money. You spend most of it and pass about $10 to your sibling, who passes on about $1. Energy works the same way. Roughly 10% reaches the next trophic level.

scenes.heading: Where does the other 90% go?
points: Parts not eaten: roots, bones, bark
scenes.say: Where does the rest go? Most is used in cellular respiration and lost as heat. Some parts, like bones and bark, aren't eaten, and some food leaves as faeces. The energy isn't destroyed. It just leaves the food chain.

scenes.heading: Using the 10% rule
scenes.question: Grass stores 50,000 kJ per square metre per year. How much energy reaches the dingo in grass → kangaroo → dingo?
lines: Only 1% of the energy in the grass
scenes.say: Grass stores fifty thousand kilojoules. Divide by ten at each step. The kangaroo gets five thousand, and the dingo gets just five hundred. That's only one percent of the energy in the grass.
scenes.caption: Grass stores 50,000 kJ. Divide by 10 at each step. The kangaroo gets 5,000, and the dingo gets just 500. That's only 1% of the energy in the grass.

scenes.heading: Energy flows, nutrients cycle
points: Energy pyramids always narrow at the top
Energy must be topped up by sunlight
scenes.say: Because energy is lost at each step, energy pyramids always narrow at the top. That's why eagles and sharks are rare, and food chains rarely go past four or five levels. Energy flows one way, but nutrients are recycled by decomposers.

points: About 10% passes to the next level
scenes.say: Quick recap. Energy enters as sunlight. About ten percent passes up each level, and most is lost as heat. Energy flows, nutrients cycle. Now try the practice questions!
